These developments underscore the ongoing challenges in containing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.

logs.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has become the fastest-growing ever, with cases surging above 1,000 and the death toll reaching 600. The outbreak has spread to new provinces including Tshopo and Haut-Uele, and the first case outside Africa has been confirmed in France. Response efforts are hampered by funding shortages, unpaid health workers, and the closure of USAID, while new diagnostic tests and treatment trials offer hope.

As a key part of its annual 'MSF Day' campaign, the exhibition will tour three locations throughout July: The Wai, Festival Walk, and TKO Plaza. It showcases real-life stories of MSF providing emergency medical humanitarian assistance to people affected by protracted conflicts and crises. The event also features an Ebola disease-themed zone, which aims to deepen public awareness and understanding of the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

logs.summary:
On August 5, 2026, a magnitude 6.4–7.0 earthquake struck off the coast of Sarangani, Davao Occidental, at 12:13 PM local time, jolting parts of Mindanao. PHIVOLCS confirmed the tremor was an aftershock of the destructive June 26 magnitude 7.8 earthquake and reported no tsunami threat. While no damage or casualties were immediately reported, several provinces suspended classes and work as a precaution, and the quake caused panic among residents.
On August 6, 2026, a magnitude 6.3 aftershock struck off Balut Island in Sarangani, Davao Occidental, along with magnitude 5.6 and 5.3 quakes, all part of the ongoing seismic sequence following the June 26 magnitude 7.8 earthquake. In related aftermath reports, police stations in areas affected by the August 5 magnitude 6.4 quake remained operational, and a crowd at a Mindanao subsidy site was rattled but no casualties were reported.

logs.summary: Throughout late July 2026, the wildfire incident in southern France's Pyrénées-Orientales area escalated dramatically amid a broader crisis of wildfires across southwestern France and Spain. Massive fires forced over 360,000 people to evacuate, with the blaze near Bordeaux prompting 84,000 to return home on July 30 as cooler weather arrived, while a separate fast-moving fire in the Var department flared on July 22. Romania extended its firefighting mission by two weeks, and French firefighters created tree-cutting firebreaks as they described the system at breaking point, with President Macron calling the situation France's biggest challenge since WWII.

incidents.summary: On August 9-10, Russia launched massive overnight strikes on Odesa with over 200 missiles and drones, killing eight, while a separate Russian strike destroyed a WHO warehouse in Ukraine. Overnight exchanges between Russia and Ukraine killed seven civilians and injured many, including a Ukrainian drone strike 600 miles inside Russia in Tatarstan that killed 13, and a drone attack in Belgorod killing five. Pope Leo renewed calls for peace, a KIIS poll found 61% of Ukrainians willing to endure the war as long as it takes, and President Zelensky warned North Korea could send up to 50,000 troops to Russia.

logs.summary:
Ukraine struck additional warehouses of Russia's top online retailer Wildberries and intensified attacks on Ozon, causing economic disruption. In leadership moves, President Zelensky replaced the commander-in-chief with Mykhailo Drapatyi and fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sparking protests. Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russia's Lavrov in Manila, expressing readiness to help end the war but noting no quick deal is imminent.
Ukrainian strikes on Russia's Wildberries warehouses produced massive pillars of black smoke as fires raged at the facilities. Russia, stretched by Ukraine's drone attacks on its Black Sea Fleet, has pulled all warships from the Mediterranean Sea. Both sides have increased bridge strikes to disrupt resupply networks, indicating expectations of a prolonged stalemate, while the Kremlin warned against optimism on peace following the Rubio-Lavrov meeting.
The EU passed its 21st sanctions package with 218 new designations targeting Russia, including vessels that refuel shadow fleet tankers. Ukrainian strikes continued to hit Russian Wildberries warehouses, while new airstrikes caused deaths in both Ukraine and Russia, and a drone was shot down over NATO airspace.

Iran toughened its demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with the Revolutionary Guards insisting the U.S. must meet conditions including compensation for war damages, even as a deal with Oman is said to be in final stages. Iran-backed Houthis attacked an Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia and a Red Sea port, while reports indicated President Trump may prioritize reopening the Strait over securing a nuclear deal with Tehran.
Iran continues to tie reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to multiple US concessions, including compensation and an end to sanctions, while nearing a final pact with Oman on temporary shipping lanes. President Trump described the US as "semi-negotiating" with Tehran, and Iran appointed hardliner Mohsen Rezaei as its new security chief amid the deadlock. Oil prices rose as traders assessed the uncertain talks.

The U.S. and Iran have paused attacks and resumed diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, with mediators reporting progress and talks focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the Pentagon quietly removed four recent troop deaths from its official Iran war death toll, reclassifying them in a new category, sparking controversy. Additional concerns include the U.S.'s dangerously low weaponry supply and growing public skepticism over the war’s costs and duration.
Mediators reported that neither the U.S. nor Iran conducted any attacks for three consecutive days, signaling progress in ceasefire efforts. New polls indicate that only one in three Americans now support the war, the lowest reading since the conflict began, and a majority view it as going "very badly." The Pentagon continued to face scrutiny over its reclassification of four troop deaths from the conflict.

logs.summary:
The conflict continues to intensify: U.S. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine is reportedly seeking an off-ramp from the war as military options remain limited, while Iran aims to block U.S. Navy ships from the Strait of Hormuz in ongoing deal talks. Houthi rebels are escalating attacks on Saudi-backed targets, and Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan as the war draws closer. Economic impacts deepen as U.S. employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, 70 ships remain trapped in the Persian Gulf, and Citi revised its Brent crude forecast to $80/bbl. The Senate passed a Russia-Iran sanctions bill, Treasury Secretary Bessent unveiled new evidence of sanctions pressure, and calls grow for a windfall tax on oil companies' massive profits, while Defense Secretary Hegseth was forced to admit the conflict is a war.
Iran displayed wreckage of U.S. aircraft lost during the conflict, as the UAE condemned Iran for attacking an ADNOC oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, reporting that 15 of its vessels have been targeted since the war began. Meanwhile, Iran stated that a deal with Oman on the Strait is close but affirmed the waterway will not reopen without meeting its conditions. The mounting financial costs of the war continue to provoke debate among U.S. lawmakers.

logs.summary:
Iran issued new sweeping demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, insisting it will not open until the U.S. corrects its behavior, while the UAE reported an Iranian missile struck an ADNOC oil tanker. The Pentagon asked arms firms to speed up output as the war exhausts supplies, and VP JD Vance said the U.S. and Iran are "in the middle of the game" as strait talks stall. Analysts describe Iran's strategy as betting that military pressure will force U.S. acceptance of its control over the waterway.
The Houthis struck an Aramco facility in Jazan and the port of Mocha in Yemen, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards stated they would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the US meets all conditions, including compensation for war damages. Separately, Egypt may join a defense pact with Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, and the Pentagon is pressing defense firms to accelerate weapons production as stocks deplete.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said on Saturday that an Iranian missile targeted one of its ships that's owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-run ADNOC oil company. No casualties were reported. Elsewhere in the region, Yemen’s military attacked the country's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in response to the strikes, escalating tensions and threatening to reignite the civil war. And Turkey's foreign minister gave new details on a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

logs.summary:
Iran toughened its demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with the Revolutionary Guards insisting the U.S. must meet conditions including compensation for war damages, even as a deal with Oman is said to be in final stages. Iran-backed Houthis attacked an Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia and a Red Sea port, while reports indicated President Trump may prioritize reopening the Strait over securing a nuclear deal with Tehran.
Iran continues to tie reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to multiple US concessions, including compensation and an end to sanctions, while nearing a final pact with Oman on temporary shipping lanes. President Trump described the US as "semi-negotiating" with Tehran, and Iran appointed hardliner Mohsen Rezaei as its new security chief amid the deadlock. Oil prices rose as traders assessed the uncertain talks.

incidents.summary: Two weeks after the earthquake, over 6,000 evacuees remain in shelters, with preparations underway to move them to hotels. The Japanese government will apply reconstruction aid law to all of Kumamoto Prefecture, offering up to ¥3 million for housing repair, while U.S. Forces airlifted 33,000 bottles of drinking water to the region. Additional aftermath reports include a fireworks display honoring victims, a survivor urging youth to pursue peace, and warnings about post-quake scams and crimes targeting damaged homes and shelters.

logs.summary:
A powerful earthquake, initially measured at magnitude 7.1 (later revised to 6.8), struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southern Japan on July 28, 2026, at 4:27 p.m. local time. The quake caused the partial collapse of the Aeon Mall in Kashima, trapping many people and leaving an unknown number dead, while injuring at least 50 others and causing widespread damage including fires, power outages, and damage to historic Kumamoto Castle.
A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan's Kyushu island near Kumamoto on July 28, 2026, causing a shopping mall to partially collapse with multiple people trapped and feared dead. The quake knocked out power to thousands of homes, ruptured roads, triggered a temporary tsunami advisory, and left dozens injured, with up to 30 mall employees missing after an explosion.

news.body: Officials say the latest victim from a powerful earthquake that struck Japan’s southwestern prefecture of Kumamoto last week is an elderly woman who apparently developed heat stroke while taking shelter in a car. The fatality came as concerns of heat-related illness grow in the area that is also suffering extreme temperatures. The magnitude 7.1 quake hit Kumamoto on Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu on Tuesday. The death toll is now 36. Authorities have ended a massive search-and-rescue operation at a collapsed shopping mall in southwest Japan after retrieving five people and the bodies of seven others over the past five days.

logs.summary: Two weeks after the earthquake, over 6,000 evacuees remain in shelters, with preparations underway to move them to hotels. The Japanese government will apply reconstruction aid law to all of Kumamoto Prefecture, offering up to ¥3 million for housing repair, while U.S. Forces airlifted 33,000 bottles of drinking water to the region. Additional aftermath reports include a fireworks display honoring victims, a survivor urging youth to pursue peace, and warnings about post-quake scams and crimes targeting damaged homes and shelters.

The heat and a lack of water have added to the challenges in the severely damaged areas. The quake killed 38 people, including one who died of apparent heat stroke while taking shelter in a car in hot weather. Residents put out heaps of debris, broken furniture and damaged appliances for collection, while in the towns of Uki and Hikawa, construction of temporary housing began.

incidents.summary:
Western Europe set a new average temperature record for the June-July period, intensifying drought conditions. Jamaica continues to grapple with drought, while Georgia’s historic drought has officially ended after nearly 11 months. In Wyoming, low water levels in Seminoe Reservoir due to drought are threatening a proposed pumped-water storage power project.
The Rhine River's water flow dropped to near an 80-year low since 1947, severely curbing shipping, while satellite images revealed unprecedented drops in Europe's Po, Loire, and other major rivers. Western Europe recorded its hottest June-July period on record, and a Triodos bank report warns extreme heat could erase EU economic growth in 2026. In the UK, a fifth heatwave is expected, with more parts of England likely to be declared in drought, while in the US, Colorado officials are releasing more water into the Arkansas River to combat drought conditions, and two Massachusetts regions exited drought status due to July rains.

logs.summary:
A severe drought is affecting multiple regions globally as of late July 2026. In Europe, an "exceptionally serious" drought has hit half of England and all of Wales, while the Rhine River dropped to its lowest ever level in the Netherlands and the Danube reached record lows in Budapest, disrupting tourism and industry. In the United States, drought conditions worsened in states like Minnesota and Michigan, while other areas like the Grand Strand in South Carolina are lifting drought management plans, and parts of Virginia and North Carolina are seeing improvements.
New drought developments include worsening conditions in Maine and Minnesota, with 35% of Minnesota in severe drought, while South Carolina's Lowcountry remains under extreme drought despite summer storms. In Europe, record-low river levels continue to disrupt power output and transport, and wildfire risk is elevated across the continent. Jamaica faces a potential $500 million drought response, and drone footage highlights the drought's impact in England.

news.headline: Record-low Danube River affects tourism and industry as drought and heat grip Central Europe
news.body: As wildfires and successive heatwaves in France and Spain highlight climate change's impact, a severe drought is causing record low water levels on the Danube River, affecting tourism and industry. The river, which flows through 10 countries, has receded to unprecedented lows, exposing rocks and old shipwrecks. In Budapest, the Danube was measured at just 23 centimeters, breaking previous records. River cruise ships are docking upriver, and sightseeing cruises have been canceled. The drought has also affected Hungary and Romania's nuclear power plant operations, exposed a World War II bomb, and ended the summer season for excursion boat operators in Serbia.

logs.summary:
Greece faced severe wildfires in late July and early August 2026, with a major blaze northwest of Athens destroying over 100 homes and burning thousands of hectares. On August 2, two firefighting helicopters collided in mid-air near Psatha, killing two crew members. By August 3, water-dropping aircraft continued to battle the fires, which had been fueled by extreme winds and record-breaking heat, with over 200 fires reported across the country since July 27.
On August 3, the wildfire west of Athens flared up again, requiring continued water-bombing aircraft operations. By August 4, firefighters seized a break in high winds to reinforce containment lines, while some residents returned to damaged homes, though forecasters warned that stronger gusts and rising temperatures were expected to return. The blaze, part of over 200 fires across Greece since late July, remained a threat amid a record-breaking heatwave and drought.

news.headline: Wildfires Rage in Greece as Heat Wave Grips Europe
news.body: In Greece, two firefighters were killed Sunday when two helicopters battling a massive wildfire collided west of Athens. Two other crew members in one of the helicopters were rescued. More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight this weekend in blazes that broke out around the coastal village of Porto Germeno. Hundreds of people have been evacuated. This is a local resident. Giorgos Mavroidis: “It’s not a good situation. This is extremely sad. The wind is very strong and keeps changing direction. It’s difficult to deal with. The firefighters, who are trained and experienced, can’t contain it. How can we?” Meanwhile, Hungary has temporarily shut down the country’s sole nuclear power plant for the first time in more than four decades amid a scorching heat wave and severe drought that triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. In more related news, Britain’s National Farmers’ Union warns rising heat and a water drought could lead to shortages of certain foods in parts of England. This is at least the third drought in five years, with some areas of England not seeing rain in over a month. Here in the United States, in Washington state, nearly 65,000 people have received evacuation orders amid intensifying wildfires around the city of Spokane. Local officials say blazes in the region have destroyed more than 700 homes and businesses.

news.headline: As France tames wildfire and lets 84,000 evacuees go home, blazes flare across Europe
news.body: France has allowed 84,000 evacuees to return home after a massive wildfire, signaling progress in battling the flames. The fire has burned an area four times the size of Paris. However, wildfires continue to flare across Europe, fueled by an exceptionally hot and dry summer. Firefighters are tackling blazes in the U.K., Spain, Germany, Greece, and Turkey. Hollywood star George Clooney evacuated his French home due to a nearby fire. In France, authorities are using water cannons and international aid to control the situation. Cooler weather and rain are helping efforts, but conditions remain challenging.

news.headline: Europe’s wildfire crisis eases in west as danger shifts east to Greece
news.body: Firefighters have contained a vast wildfire in southwestern France, allowing nearly 200,000 people to return home. The development comes after what may have been the country’s largest peacetime evacuation. However, renewed fires have forced thousands from their homes in other parts of France and Greece. In the Var region, a fire thought to be under control raced across 10 square kilometers in just six hours. Meanwhile, in Greece, gale-force winds have driven flames through the coastal area between Athens and Thebes, leading to evacuations. Rising temperatures and prolonged droughts are making Europe more vulnerable to such wildfires.

news.headline: 2 killed when firefighting helicopters collide near Athens as Europe’s wildfire emergency rages
news.body: Greece’s fire department says the collision of two firefighting helicopters battling a major wildfire burning out of control west of Athens left two crew members dead, while another two were recovered alive. The fire department said on Sunday the dead crew members were one Greek and one Danish national, while the two who were recovered alive were one Greek and one British national. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires during the country’s hot, dry summers. The collision laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe’s wildfire emergency.
